passage:
At two, Tanvir covered his eyes with both hands on the sofa and announced, "Can't see me!" Ayesha, his mother, played along. "Where's Tanvir?" Later he held a picture book with the cover facing himself and showed her the back. "Look, dog!"

At ten, Chaitanya wanted cricket at break while Tanvir wanted marbles. Tanvir knew Chaitanya liked different things and even offered to play cricket first, but when Chaitanya won the toss for the bat, Tanvir's face flushed and he stomped off shouting, "You always get your way!"

At fifteen, after a bad haircut, Tanvir sat in the back of the auto with his hood up. "Nobody has ever felt like this," he muttered. "Everyone is staring at me." The woman across the aisle was reading her phone. Ayesha said, "I had a haircut disaster at your age, worse than this." Tanvir groaned, but he glanced at her.

qa.q: What did Tanvir say when he covered his eyes at two?
How does Tanvir's understanding of other people's views change from two to fifteen?
qa.a: At two he covers his eyes and thinks nobody can see him, at ten he knows Chaitanya likes different things but stomps off when his own feelings run high, and at fifteen he feels that nobody has felt this before and everyone is staring. His sense of other minds grows, yet strong feelings still narrow it.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling in the auto with his hood up?
qa.a: Tanvir felt self-conscious and alone, sure that his bad haircut was on everyone's mind.

qa.q: What could Ayesha do next to help Tanvir feel less alone?
qa.a: Ayesha could keep sharing small stories of her own mistakes and listen without teasing, so Tanvir sees that others have felt this too. 🙂

grounding: A boy's view that only his own view exists at two, half-grown sense of other minds at ten, and belief that everyone watches him at fifteen show egocentrism softening.
